title: LLM basics & calling APIs
scopeHtml: Scope: What an LLM is, tokens and the context window, messages and roles, generation parameters, a first API call, usage and cost, errors and retries, streaming, multi-turn state, and basic model choice.

notes.title: What an LLM actually is
notes.html:
A large language model (LLM) is a program that has read an enormous amount of text and learned one trick: given some text, predict what text most likely comes next. That is all. When you chat with Claude or ChatGPT, the model is repeatedly answering the question "given everything so far, what is the next small piece of text?", appending that piece, and asking again until it decides to stop.

Some words you will hear constantly, defined once:

  • Model: the trained file of numbers (called weights or parameters, often billions of them) that does the predicting. You do not run it yourself; a provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) hosts it and you call it over the internet.
  • Prompt: the text you send in. It includes your question, instructions and any documents you paste.
  • Completion / response: the text the model sends back.
  • Inference: running a trained model to get an answer (as opposed to training, which builds the model and costs millions).
  • Stateless: the model remembers nothing between calls. Every request must carry the full context again. This one fact explains half of the design decisions in this whole topic.

How training works in one paragraph: the model first reads huge amounts of text (pre-training) and learns language, facts and patterns. Then it is tuned with human feedback and examples (post-training, e.g. instruction tuning and RLHF) so that it behaves like a helpful assistant instead of just continuing random text. You do not do either of these as an app developer; you consume the finished model through an API (Application Programming Interface: an HTTPS endpoint you send JSON to).

What LLMs are good at: summarising, rewriting, extracting fields from messy text, classifying, translating, explaining code, drafting, answering questions about text you provide. What they are bad at without help: exact arithmetic, knowing today's news, knowing your private data, and being 100 percent factual. They can hallucinate: produce fluent, confident, wrong text, because they optimise for "plausible next text", not "true text".

Real products using this exact setup:

  • GitHub Copilot sends your surrounding code as the prompt and shows the predicted continuation.
  • Gmail Smart Compose / "Help me write" sends your draft plus an instruction and shows the completion.
  • Swiggy- or Zomato-style support bots send the customer message plus order data to an LLM and show its reply.
  • Notion AI sends the page text and an instruction such as "summarise this".

Analogy: think of a phone keyboard's autocomplete that has read the entire internet and can keep going for pages. It does not "know" anything the way you do; it is extremely good at continuing text in a believable way. And like a person with amnesia and a notepad, it only knows what is written on the notepad (the prompt) you hand it each time.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the model remembers the conversation". It does not; the client resends history every call.
  • Saying "the model looks up facts in a database". It generates from learned patterns; any lookup is something you add around it (RAG, tools).
  • Confusing training with inference, or thinking your API calls train the model (by default they do not; check the provider's data policy).
  • Treating confident output as correct. Hallucination is a property you must design around, not a bug that will be "fixed".

notes.title: Tokens and the context window
notes.html:
Models do not read letters or words. They read tokens: chunks of text produced by a tokenizer. A token can be a whole common word ("the"), part of a word ("un", "believ", "able"), a single character or punctuation, or a piece of whitespace. In English, one token is roughly 4 characters or about 0.75 words, so 1,000 tokens is around 750 words. Other languages (Hindi, Chinese, Arabic) and code often use more tokens per word. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so the same text can have different token counts on different models; never assume, measure (see the usage section).

Why tokens matter to you as a developer:

  1. Cost: you are billed per token, with a separate (usually higher) price for output tokens than input tokens. Prices change often, so look them up on the provider's pricing page ("verify").
  2. Latency: output is produced one token at a time, so a 1,000-token answer takes about ten times longer than a 100-token one.
  3. Limits: the model can only handle a limited number of tokens at once.

The context window is that limit: the maximum number of tokens the model can consider in a single request, counting your input (system prompt, history, documents) AND the output it generates. Think of it as the model's working desk. If your input is 150,000 tokens and the window is 200,000, you only have room for about 50,000 tokens of reply. Windows have grown from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands and beyond for some models (exact sizes: verify in the model docs). If you exceed the window the API rejects the request with an error (typically a 400 invalid-request error) or you must truncate or summarise.

A separate limit is max output tokens: the cap on how long a single reply may be, which is usually smaller than the context window.

|<-------------------- context window (e.g. 200k tokens) -------------------->|
| system prompt | history | your documents | question |  model's reply (output) |
|<------------------- input tokens ---------------->|<--- output tokens ----->|

Counting tokens before you send (so you can budget):

# Python: Anthropic exposes a token-counting endpoint (verify in SDK docs for your version)
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How many tokens is this sentence?"}],
)
print(count.input_tokens)  # prints an integer such as 14
// Kotlin: use the Java SDK; count-tokens method name varies by SDK version (verify in SDK docs)
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCountTokensParams

fun main() {
    val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv() // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    val params = MessageCountTokensParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
        .addUserMessage("How many tokens is this sentence?")
        .build()
    println(client.messages().countTokens(params).inputTokens()) // prints an integer
}
// Java: same Java SDK (verify exact class and method names for your SDK version)
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCountTokensParams;

public class CountTokens {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        MessageCountTokensParams params = MessageCountTokensParams.builder()
            .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
            .addUserMessage("How many tokens is this sentence?")
            .build();
        System.out.println(client.messages().countTokens(params).inputTokens()); // prints an integer
    }
}

Real-world examples: ChatGPT and Claude.ai show "this conversation is too long" or silently drop old messages when the window fills; Cursor and Copilot choose which files to include in the prompt precisely because the window is finite; document-chat products split PDFs into pieces for the same reason.

Analogy: tokens are like Lego bricks; the model builds and reads in bricks, not in whole sentences. The context window is the size of the table the model builds on: everything you give it plus everything it writes must fit on that one table.

Common interview traps.

  • "1 token = 1 word". It is roughly 0.75 English words, and varies by language and tokenizer.
  • Forgetting the window includes output tokens, so a full-window prompt leaves no room to answer.
  • Assuming a bigger window means better answers. Very long inputs cost more, are slower, and models can miss details buried in the middle.
  • Counting tokens with your own character math in production instead of using the provider's counter or the usage field.

notes.title: Messages, roles and the system prompt
notes.html:
Modern chat APIs do not take one big string. They take a list of messages, each with a role and content:

  • system: instructions that set behaviour for the whole conversation ("You are a polite support agent for ShopX. Answer in two sentences."). The model treats it as higher-priority guidance. On the Anthropic API the system prompt is a separate top-level system parameter, not an item in the messages list; on OpenAI-compatible APIs it is a message with role system (or developer on newer models; verify).
  • user: what the human (or your app on their behalf) says.
  • assistant: what the model said earlier. You include past assistant messages in the list so the model can see the conversation so far. You can also pre-fill an assistant message to steer the start of the reply on some APIs (verify support).

Messages must follow the API's rules: on Anthropic they alternate user/assistant and start with a user message. The model's reply comes back as a new assistant message made of one or more content blocks (usually a single text block; also tool-use blocks, covered in later topics).

system  : "You are a terse SQL tutor."
messages: [ user: "What is a JOIN?" ]
                   |
                   v   (HTTPS POST /v1/messages)
            [   LLM   ]
                   |
                   v
response: assistant: "A JOIN combines rows from two tables on a key."

Why the system prompt exists: it separates your fixed rules (tone, format, safety limits, role) from the changing user input. Put stable instructions there; put the variable question in a user message. This is also where you tell the model what NOT to do. Remember that users can try to override it ("ignore previous instructions"); this is prompt injection, covered in the prompts topic, so never put secrets in a system prompt.

Real-world examples: a banking chatbot's system prompt says "never reveal account numbers, redirect to the secure page"; Duolingo-style tutors use a system prompt that fixes the persona and level; customer-support copilots inject company policy into the system prompt and the ticket text into the user message.

Analogy: the system prompt is the employee handbook given on day one, the user messages are customers walking up to the counter, and the assistant messages are the employee's earlier answers written in the logbook.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting the system prompt inside messages on the Anthropic API (it has its own system field) or forgetting the first message must be from the user.
  • Believing the system prompt is secret or unbreakable. Treat it as guidance that can leak or be bypassed.
  • Not knowing that the model never "sees" roles as separate channels; they are formatted into one token stream internally.
  • Sending two user messages in a row on an API that requires alternation (you get a 400 error).

notes.title: Your first API call
notes.html:
You need three things: an API key (a secret string from the provider's console that identifies and bills you), an endpoint URL, and a JSON body. The key goes in a header, never in source code or in a mobile app. Read it from an environment variable such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; the official SDKs do this automatically.

The raw REST request to Anthropic's Messages API looks like this:

POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
Headers:
  x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  anthropic-version: 2023-06-01
  content-type: application/json
Body:
  { "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5",
    "max_tokens": 256,
    "system": "You are a concise assistant.",
    "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Explain DNS in one sentence."} ] }

max_tokens is required on the Anthropic API. The reply JSON contains content (a list of blocks, the text is in the first block), stop_reason (why it stopped), usage (token counts) and id. Do not hand-roll the body in production if an SDK exists; use the SDK for typing, retries and error classes. Model ids change over time, so confirm the current id in the provider's model list ("verify").

# Python SDK: pip install anthropic
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=256,
    system="You are a concise assistant.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain DNS in one sentence."}],
)
print(response.content[0].text)  # prints e.g. "DNS translates domain names into IP addresses."
print(response.stop_reason)      # prints "end_turn"
// Kotlin using the Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java); verify builder names in the SDK docs
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams

fun main() {
    val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv() // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
        .maxTokens(256)
        .system("You are a concise assistant.")
        .addUserMessage("Explain DNS in one sentence.")
        .build()
    val message = client.messages().create(params)
    message.content().forEach { block ->
        block.text().ifPresent { println(it.text()) } // prints the model's sentence
    }
}
// Java using com.anthropic:anthropic-java (verify builder and accessor names in the SDK docs)
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.Message;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams;

public class FirstCall {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
            .maxTokens(256)
            .system("You are a concise assistant.")
            .addUserMessage("Explain DNS in one sentence.")
            .build();
        Message message = client.messages().create(params);
        message.content().forEach(b -> b.text().ifPresent(t -> System.out.println(t.text())));
        // prints the model's one-sentence answer
    }
}

The same shape works elsewhere. OpenAI-compatible servers (OpenAI, many open-source hosts, local Ollama at http://localhost:11434/v1) use POST /v1/chat/completions with messages including a system role, and return choices[0].message.content. Google Gemini uses generateContent with contents and parts. The concepts are identical; only field names differ. Because of this, many teams put a thin interface of their own in front of the provider so swapping models is a one-file change.

Real-world examples: Stripe-style apps generate invoice summaries with this one call; Perplexity-like apps wrap the call with search results; Jira and Slack AI features are this call plus product context. Typical hosted-model latency for a short reply is on the order of a second or two (varies widely; measure it).

Analogy: calling the API is like ordering from a restaurant by sending a written slip through the pass window. You write the table rules on top (system), the dish request below (user), and the kitchen (the hosted model) hands back one plate. The kitchen does not remember you walked in earlier.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard-coding the API key or committing it to Git. Use env vars or a secrets manager; rotate leaked keys immediately.
  • Forgetting max_tokens on Anthropic (request fails) or reading content as a plain string instead of a list of blocks.
  • Calling the LLM directly from a mobile app. The key would ship in the APK; call your own backend instead.
  • Assuming the same model id or parameter exists across providers or versions.

notes.title: Generation parameters
notes.html:
The model does not output one answer; at each step it produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens, and a sampling step picks one. Parameters control how.

Parameter What it does Typical use
max_tokens Hard cap on output tokens. Output is cut off when hit (stop_reason = max_tokens). Always set it; protects cost and latency.
temperature Randomness. Near 0 = pick the most likely token (focused, repeatable-ish). Higher = more varied and creative. Low for extraction, classification, code; higher for brainstorming.
top_p (nucleus sampling) Sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Alternative to temperature; adjust one, not both.
top_k Sample only from the k most likely tokens (not on every API). Rarely needed.
stop_sequences / stop Strings that end generation as soon as produced (the stop text itself is not returned). Cut at "\n\nUser:" or a closing tag.

Important details:

  • Temperature 0 is not a guarantee of identical output every time; it reduces variance but hosted systems can still differ slightly. Never build logic that needs bit-exact repeats. Some providers have a seed for best-effort reproducibility; Anthropic's API does not offer the same guarantee (verify).
  • Some newer reasoning-oriented models restrict or ignore sampling parameters like temperature; always check the current docs for the specific model ("verify").
  • max_tokens counts only the reply. If you set it too low, the answer is truncated mid-sentence and JSON output becomes invalid; check stop_reason.
  • Higher temperature does not mean "smarter" or "more creative about facts"; it means more risk of odd or wrong tokens.
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=100,
    temperature=0.2,                 # focused answer
    stop_sequences=["\n\n"],         # stop at the first blank line
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name three Android lifecycle callbacks."}],
)
print(response.stop_reason)  # "stop_sequence" if a blank line ended it, "max_tokens" if cut, else "end_turn"
val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
    .maxTokens(100)
    .temperature(0.2)                       // focused answer
    .addStopSequence("\n\n")                // stop at the first blank line
    .addUserMessage("Name three Android lifecycle callbacks.")
    .build()
val msg = client.messages().create(params)
println(msg.stopReason()) // prints the stop reason (end_turn, max_tokens or stop_sequence)
MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
    .maxTokens(100)
    .temperature(0.2)                       // focused answer
    .addStopSequence("\n\n")                // stop at the first blank line
    .addUserMessage("Name three Android lifecycle callbacks.")
    .build();
Message msg = client.messages().create(params);
System.out.println(msg.stopReason()); // prints the stop reason (verify accessor in SDK docs)

Real-world examples: Grammarly-like extraction and classification pipelines use temperature near 0; marketing-copy tools (Jasper, Copy.ai style) raise it for variety; code assistants keep it low; chat apps cap max_tokens per reply to control cost.

Analogy: temperature is a dial on a jukebox. At zero it always plays the most popular song; turned up, it sometimes plays a surprising track from further down the chart. max_tokens is the song-length limit, and a stop sequence is a "stop when you hear this word" rule.

Common interview traps.

  • "Temperature 0 is deterministic." It is nearly, not guaranteed.
  • Setting both temperature and top_p aggressively; most guides recommend changing only one.
  • Ignoring stop_reason == max_tokens and parsing a truncated JSON blob.
  • Thinking high temperature fixes repetitive or bad answers; usually the prompt needs fixing.

notes.title: Reading the response, usage and cost
notes.html:
Every response tells you what it cost. The usage object reports input tokens (what you sent) and output tokens (what the model produced); some APIs also report cache-related counts (cache creation and cache read tokens) when prompt caching is used (covered in the production topic). Always log these per request. Cost is:

cost = input_tokens  * price_per_input_token
     + output_tokens * price_per_output_token

Output tokens are usually several times more expensive than input tokens, and prices differ per model (small fast models cost much less than large ones). Look up current prices on the pricing page ("verify"); never hard-code them without a config file.

Fields to read on every call:

  • content: the generated blocks.
  • stop_reason: end_turn (finished naturally), max_tokens (truncated), stop_sequence, and tool_use (the model wants to call a tool).
  • usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens.
  • id and the request id header: log them so you can report issues to the provider.
  • model: the exact model that served the request.
u = response.usage
print(u.input_tokens, u.output_tokens)        # e.g. 42 118
# example per-million-token prices are placeholders; load real ones from config (verify)
cost = u.input_tokens * 3 / 1_000_000 + u.output_tokens * 15 / 1_000_000
print(f"${cost:.6f}")                          # e.g. $0.001896
val usage = message.usage()
println("${usage.inputTokens()} ${usage.outputTokens()}") // e.g. 42 118
// placeholder prices per million tokens; load real ones from config (verify)
val cost = usage.inputTokens() * 3.0 / 1_000_000 + usage.outputTokens() * 15.0 / 1_000_000
println("%.6f".format(cost)) // e.g. 0.001896
Usage usage = message.usage(); // com.anthropic.models.messages.Usage
System.out.println(usage.inputTokens() + " " + usage.outputTokens()); // e.g. 42 118
// placeholder prices per million tokens; load real ones from config (verify)
double cost = usage.inputTokens() * 3.0 / 1_000_000 + usage.outputTokens() * 15.0 / 1_000_000;
System.out.printf("%.6f%n", cost); // e.g. 0.001896

Cost levers you will meet later: shorter prompts, cheaper models for easy tasks, lower max_tokens, prompt caching for repeated prefixes, batch APIs for non-urgent work, and caching whole responses. Because history is resent every turn, a long conversation's cost grows roughly quadratically if you never trim it.

Real-world examples: SaaS products with AI features keep a per-user token ledger (so the free tier can be capped); FinOps dashboards in Datadog or Langfuse chart tokens per feature; teams alert when average input tokens per request jumps (usually someone pasted a huge document into the prompt).

Analogy: the usage field is the itemised receipt after a taxi ride: tokens in are the distance to the pickup, tokens out are the distance driven with the passenger, and the meter rate differs for each.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating cost from word counts rather than the reported token counts.
  • Forgetting that every turn resends the whole history, so cost per turn rises as the chat grows.
  • Ignoring output pricing, which is usually the bigger multiplier.
  • Not logging usage and request ids, then being unable to debug a bill or a support ticket.

notes.title: Errors, status codes and retries
notes.html:
API calls fail; plan for it. The status code tells you what to do.

Status Meaning What to do
400 Invalid request (bad JSON, missing max_tokens, too many tokens, bad role order) Fix the request. Do not retry blindly.
401 Missing or wrong API key Check the key and header. No retry.
403 Key lacks permission for the resource Fix permissions or the model name.
404 Unknown model or endpoint Check the model id spelling and availability.
413 Request body too large Shrink it.
429 Rate limit exceeded (too many requests or tokens per minute) Wait and retry with backoff; honour the retry-after header.
500 Provider internal error Retry with backoff.
529 (Anthropic) / 503 Provider overloaded or unavailable Retry with backoff, then fall back to another model.
Timeout / connection error Network or slow generation Retry with backoff; set explicit timeouts.

Rule of thumb: 4xx (except 429) are your fault, do not retry; 429 and 5xx are transient, retry. Use exponential backoff with jitter: wait about 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, ... plus a random amount, up to a small maximum number of attempts. Jitter stops thousands of clients retrying in lockstep. Official SDKs already retry some errors a couple of times by default and let you configure max_retries and timeouts (verify defaults in the SDK docs). Also set a timeout: long generations can take tens of seconds, so use a generous read timeout or streaming.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=3, timeout=60.0)  # SDK-level retries and timeout
try:
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=200,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])
    print(r.content[0].text)
except anthropic.RateLimitError:            # 429
    print("slow down")                      # retries were exhausted; back off or queue
except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:       # other 4xx/5xx
    print(e.status_code, e.message)         # e.g. 400 plus the provider's error text
except anthropic.APIConnectionError:
    print("network problem")
import com.anthropic.errors.AnthropicException
import com.anthropic.errors.RateLimitException

val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.builder()
    .fromEnv()
    .maxRetries(3)                              // SDK-level retries (verify builder options)
    .build()
try {
    val m = client.messages().create(params)
    println(m.content())
} catch (e: RateLimitException) {               // 429
    println("slow down")
} catch (e: AnthropicException) {               // base class for other SDK errors
    println("API error: ${e.message}")          // prints the provider's error text
}
import com.anthropic.errors.AnthropicException;
import com.anthropic.errors.RateLimitException;

AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.builder()
    .fromEnv()
    .maxRetries(3)                              // SDK-level retries (verify builder options)
    .build();
try {
    Message m = client.messages().create(params);
    System.out.println(m.content());
} catch (RateLimitException e) {                // 429
    System.out.println("slow down");
} catch (AnthropicException e) {                // base class for other SDK errors
    System.out.println("API error: " + e.getMessage());
}

Also handle non-HTTP failures: the call succeeds (200) but the answer is unusable: truncated (max_tokens), refused, or not in the format you asked for. Check stop_reason and validate the output.

Real-world examples: any production chatbot (Intercom Fin, Zendesk AI) wraps calls in retry plus fallback to a second model or a canned message; during big provider incidents, apps degrade gracefully ("AI is busy, try again") instead of crashing; Android apps show a retry button because their backend proxy returns a 503.

Analogy: a 429 is a busy restaurant host saying "full, come back in ten minutes"; retrying every second just annoys the queue, while waiting a bit longer each time (and not arriving in a crowd at the exact same minute) gets you a table. A 400 is ordering something not on the menu; asking again will not help.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying 400/401 errors in a loop (never succeeds, costs money, burns rate limit).
  • Retrying without backoff or jitter, creating a retry storm that makes an outage worse.
  • Not setting timeouts, so a hung request blocks a thread or a UI.
  • Retrying non-idempotent side effects (e.g., calling a tool that sends email) because the LLM request failed halfway.

notes.title: Streaming responses
notes.html:
A long answer can take 10 to 30 seconds to complete. If you wait for the whole thing, the user stares at a spinner. Streaming sends tokens as they are generated so the UI can show text immediately. The metric that matters is time to first token (TTFT), usually well under a second or two, instead of total time.

The wire format is Server-Sent Events (SSE): one long-lived HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream where the server writes small events as they happen. Each event has an event: name and a data: JSON line. You request it by adding "stream": true. Anthropic's event types, in order, are roughly:

message_start          -> metadata, input token usage
content_block_start    -> a text block begins
content_block_delta    -> {"delta": {"type":"text_delta","text":"Hel"}}   (repeated many times)
content_block_stop     -> block finished
message_delta          -> stop_reason and final output token usage
message_stop           -> stream ends
(ping events may appear; errors can arrive mid-stream as an "error" event)

OpenAI-compatible APIs stream data: {...} chunks with choices[0].delta.content and end with data: [DONE]. SDKs hide the parsing and give you a text iterator or callbacks.

Things that go wrong: the connection can drop mid-answer, so you may have partial text; a mid-stream error arrives after the 200 status has already been sent, so you cannot rely on the status code alone; proxies and load balancers that buffer responses will break streaming (disable buffering, e.g., X-Accel-Buffering: no on nginx); JSON output cannot be parsed until complete.

with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about Gradle."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:        # yields small text chunks
        print(text, end="", flush=True)    # prints the haiku progressively
    final = stream.get_final_message()     # full message with usage
print(final.usage.output_tokens)
// Java SDK streaming from Kotlin (verify class names in the SDK docs)
client.messages().createStreaming(params).use { response ->
    response.stream().forEach { event ->
        event.contentBlockDelta().ifPresent { delta ->
            delta.delta().text().ifPresent { print(it.text()) } // prints chunks as they arrive
        }
    }
}
// Java SDK streaming (verify class names in the SDK docs)
try (StreamResponse<RawMessageStreamEvent> response = client.messages().createStreaming(params)) {
    response.stream().forEach(event ->
        event.contentBlockDelta().ifPresent(delta ->
            delta.delta().text().ifPresent(t -> System.out.print(t.text())))); // prints chunks as they arrive
}

On Android, you would not stream from the LLM straight to the phone; your backend streams SSE to the app (OkHttp's SSE support, or Ktor), and you expose it as a Kotlin Flow<String> that Compose collects. That belongs to the Android/JVM topic later.

Real-world examples: ChatGPT, Claude.ai and Gemini all type out answers via SSE; Cursor streams code edits; Perplexity streams the answer while citations arrive; voice assistants start text-to-speech on the first sentence to cut perceived latency.

Analogy: non-streaming is waiting for a whole parcel to be packed before it is sent; streaming is a conveyor belt delivering items one by one as they come off the production line, so you can start unpacking right away.

Common interview traps.

  • Streaming does not make the model faster overall; it improves perceived latency (TTFT).
  • Assuming a 200 status means the stream succeeded. Errors and cut-offs can happen mid-stream.
  • Proxy or CDN buffering silently turning your stream into one big delayed chunk.
  • Parsing partial JSON from a stream, or billing/logging usage from the first event instead of the final one.

notes.title: Multi-turn conversations and state
notes.html:
Because the model is stateless, a "conversation" is something your code builds. You keep a list of messages, append the user's new message, send the entire list, then append the model's reply to the list and keep it for the next turn.

turn 1 send: [U1]                      -> reply A1
turn 2 send: [U1, A1, U2]              -> reply A2
turn 3 send: [U1, A1, U2, A2, U3]      -> reply A3
         ^ the whole history is re-sent and re-billed every time

Where state lives: in memory for a demo; in a database or Redis keyed by conversation id for a real app; on the client for a trivial app (but then validate it server-side). You decide which messages to send:

  • Sliding window: keep only the last N turns.
  • Summarisation: ask a model to summarise old turns into a short note, keep the note plus recent turns.
  • Token budget: drop the oldest turns until the total fits under a limit (leave room for the reply).
  • Retrieval: store past facts and fetch relevant ones (memory/RAG, later topics).

Keep the system prompt on every call. Never drop it when trimming.

history = []  # list of {"role", "content"}

def chat(user_text: str) -> str:
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    r = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
        system="You are a friendly tutor.", messages=history[-20:],  # sliding window
    )
    reply = r.content[0].text
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

print(chat("My name is Asha."))
print(chat("What is my name?"))   # prints a reply that mentions Asha, because history was resent
val history = mutableListOf<MessageParam>()

fun chat(userText: String): String {
    history += MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.USER).content(userText).build()
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(300)
        .system("You are a friendly tutor.")
        .messages(history.takeLast(20))                      // sliding window
        .build()
    val reply = client.messages().create(params).content()
        .mapNotNull { it.text().orElse(null)?.text() }.joinToString("")
    history += MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.ASSISTANT).content(reply).build()
    return reply
}

fun main() {
    println(chat("My name is Asha."))
    println(chat("What is my name?")) // mentions Asha because history was resent
}
List<MessageParam> history = new ArrayList<>();

String chat(String userText) {
    history.add(MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.USER).content(userText).build());
    int from = Math.max(0, history.size() - 20);             // sliding window
    MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(300)
        .system("You are a friendly tutor.")
        .messages(new ArrayList<>(history.subList(from, history.size())))
        .build();
    StringBuilder reply = new StringBuilder();
    client.messages().create(params).content()
        .forEach(b -> b.text().ifPresent(t -> reply.append(t.text())));
    history.add(MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.ASSISTANT).content(reply.toString()).build());
    return reply.toString(); // second call mentions "Asha" because history was resent
}
// builder and enum names: verify in the SDK docs

Production notes: a sliding window of N messages can cut a pair in half (starting with an assistant message breaks role rules on some APIs); store per-user conversations separately so one user's history never leaks into another's request; set a maximum conversation length or force "new chat" to cap cost; and redact personal data before storing.

Real-world examples: ChatGPT's sidebar conversations are rows in a database replayed on each turn; support bots like Intercom Fin pass the last several messages plus the customer's account data; Claude.ai and ChatGPT summarise or truncate old messages when you approach the limit; some apps add "memory" features by storing extracted facts separately.

Analogy: talking to the model is like writing letters to a pen pal with total amnesia. To keep the conversation going, every new letter must include a photocopy of all the previous letters (or a neat summary of them), otherwise they reply "who are you?".

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the API "keeps session state". It does not (the provider-side stateful APIs some vendors offer are the exception; know which you use).
  • Letting history grow unbounded: rising cost, latency and eventually a context-window error.
  • Trimming from the front and accidentally dropping the system prompt or breaking user/assistant alternation.
  • Sharing one global history list across users in a server (a classic data-leak bug).

notes.title: Choosing a model and basic trade-offs
notes.html:
There is no single best model. Providers ship a family at different sizes, trading quality/reasoning against speed and cost. A common pattern with Anthropic (verify the current lineup and ids): a small fast tier (claude-haiku-5-5), a balanced tier (claude-sonnet-5-5), and a most-capable tier (claude-opus-5-5), with claude-fable-5-1 as another option in this course's notes. Other vendors offer similar small/medium/large ladders, and open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen via Ollama or vLLM) can run on your own hardware.

How to choose, step by step:

  1. Write down the task and what "good" means (accuracy on 50 real examples beats gut feeling).
  2. Start with the balanced tier. If quality is fine, try the small tier to save money and latency; if quality is short, go up a tier.
  3. Check the constraints: context window (can the documents fit?), latency (interactive chat vs overnight batch), cost per request at your expected volume, modalities (images, PDFs, audio), tool use and structured output support, data residency and privacy terms, and availability/rate limits.
  4. Use different models for different steps: a small model to classify the question or route it, a larger one only for hard questions (model routing, covered in the production topic).
  5. Re-evaluate when new models release; pin a specific model id in production instead of an alias that silently changes behaviour, and run your test set before upgrading.
Need Lean towards
Cheap, fast, high volume (classify, extract, autocomplete) Small tier
General product features, coding, summarising Balanced tier
Hard reasoning, long agentic tasks, tricky code Largest tier
Private data that cannot leave your network Self-hosted open-weight model
Offline on a phone On-device model (Gemini Nano, MediaPipe LLM; later topic)

Real-world examples: Duolingo and Notion mix model sizes by feature; Cursor routes quick edits to small fast models and hard refactors to bigger ones; many support bots answer with a small model and escalate to a large one when confidence is low; enterprises with strict privacy run open models on their own GPUs.

Analogy: choosing a model is like choosing transport: a bicycle (small model) is cheap and fast for short trips, a car (balanced) handles most days, a truck (largest) is overkill for groceries but necessary for a house move. You would not rent a truck to buy milk.

Common interview traps.

  • "Always use the biggest model." It is slower and costlier, and often unnecessary.
  • Choosing by leaderboard instead of testing on your own data.
  • Using a floating alias in production, so behaviour changes without a deploy.
  • Ignoring context window, latency and rate limits when comparing models, looking only at quality.

notes.title: A small end-to-end CLI chatbot
notes.html:
Putting the pieces together: read the key from the environment, keep a bounded history, stream the reply, log usage, and handle errors. This is the skeleton of nearly every LLM feature.

user input -> append to history -> trim -> call API (stream) -> print tokens
                    ^                                              |
                    +---- append assistant reply <-----------------+
                                  log usage, handle errors
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=3, timeout=60.0)
history = []

while True:
    text = input("you> ")
    if text in ("quit", "exit"):
        break
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": text})
    try:
        with client.messages.stream(
            model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=400,
            system="Be brief.", messages=history[-20:],
        ) as stream:
            for chunk in stream.text_stream:
                print(chunk, end="", flush=True)
            msg = stream.get_final_message()
        history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": msg.content[0].text})
        print(f"\n[in={msg.usage.input_tokens} out={msg.usage.output_tokens}]")  # usage line
    except anthropic.APIError as e:
        history.pop()                      # drop the unanswered user turn
        print("error:", e)
fun main() {
    val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.builder().fromEnv().maxRetries(3).build()
    val history = mutableListOf<MessageParam>()
    while (true) {
        print("you> ")
        val text = readlnOrNull() ?: break
        if (text == "quit") break
        history += MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.USER).content(text).build()
        try {
            val params = MessageCreateParams.builder().model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(400)
                .system("Be brief.").messages(history.takeLast(20)).build()
            val sb = StringBuilder()
            client.messages().createStreaming(params).use { r ->
                r.stream().forEach { ev ->
                    ev.contentBlockDelta().ifPresent { d ->
                        d.delta().text().ifPresent { print(it.text()); sb.append(it.text()) }
                    }
                }
            }
            history += MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.ASSISTANT).content(sb.toString()).build()
            println()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            history.removeLast()   // drop the unanswered user turn
            println("error: ${e.message}")
        }
    }
}
public class Chat {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.builder().fromEnv().maxRetries(3).build();
        List<MessageParam> history = new ArrayList<>();
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);
        while (true) {
            System.out.print("you> ");
            String text = in.nextLine();
            if (text.equals("quit")) break;
            history.add(MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.USER).content(text).build());
            try {
                int from = Math.max(0, history.size() - 20);
                MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
                    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(400).system("Be brief.")
                    .messages(new ArrayList<>(history.subList(from, history.size()))).build();
                StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
                try (StreamResponse<RawMessageStreamEvent> r = client.messages().createStreaming(params)) {
                    r.stream().forEach(ev -> ev.contentBlockDelta().ifPresent(d ->
                        d.delta().text().ifPresent(t -> { System.out.print(t.text()); sb.append(t.text()); })));
                }
                history.add(MessageParam.builder().role(MessageParam.Role.ASSISTANT).content(sb.toString()).build());
                System.out.println();
            } catch (Exception e) {
                history.remove(history.size() - 1); // drop the unanswered user turn
                System.out.println("error: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}
// SDK class and method names throughout: verify against the current anthropic-java docs

What to add before shipping this to real users: a backend in front (auth, per-user rate limits, key kept server-side), token and cost metering, request timeouts, content safety checks, logging with request ids (without leaking personal data), and tests that call a fake client rather than the paid API.

Real-world examples: internal "ask the wiki" bots, Slack bots and CLI tools like Claude Code all follow this exact loop (history, call, stream, tool/side effects, log); mobile apps put an HTTP endpoint of your own in the middle.

Analogy: this is the cashier loop at a counter: take the order, check the ticket history, send it to the kitchen, hand dishes over as they come out, note what it cost, and apologise politely if the kitchen is down.

Common interview traps.

  • Appending the user message to history and not removing it after a failure, leaving two user messages in a row.
  • Forgetting to flush output when streaming to a terminal or HTTP response.
  • Unit tests that call the real paid API; use a fake/mock client and a small set of recorded or live evals separately.
  • Shipping the CLI pattern to mobile as-is, with the key inside the app.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An LLM predicts the next token; it is stateless, can hallucinate, and you reach it through a hosted HTTPS API using a secret key kept in an environment variable (never in an app).
  • Text is split into tokens; you pay per input and output token, latency scales with output tokens, and the context window caps input plus output together.
  • A request is a system prompt plus alternating user/assistant messages; the response is a list of content blocks plus stop_reason and usage.
  • Parameters shape output: max_tokens caps length (always set it, always check for truncation), temperature/top_p control randomness (not fully deterministic even at 0), stop_sequences end generation early.
  • Always read and log usage and request ids; cost is input tokens times input price plus output tokens times (higher) output price; history is resent every turn.
  • Handle errors by class: fix 4xx, retry 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff and jitter, set timeouts, and validate 200 responses too.
  • Streaming (SSE) improves perceived latency by sending token deltas; beware mid-stream errors and proxy buffering.
  • Conversations are state you manage: resend history, bound it (window, summary, token budget), keep the system prompt, isolate per user.
  • Pick models by testing on your own data: small for cheap and fast, balanced for most work, largest for hard tasks; pin model ids and re-evaluate on upgrades.
  • SDK method names change between versions; confirm exact classes, builders and model ids in the current Anthropic Python and Java SDK docs.

questions.promptHtml: In plain words, what is a large language model, and what is it actually doing when I send it a prompt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you have a correct mental model (next-token prediction) rather than "it is a database" or "it thinks". Every later design decision builds on it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM is a program with billions of learned numbers (weights) that has read huge amounts of text and learned to predict the most likely next small piece of text, called a token. When I send a prompt, it predicts one token, appends it, predicts the next, and repeats until it decides to stop. It generates plausible text from learned patterns; it does not look facts up, which is why it can hallucinate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Define the words first. A model is the trained file of weights, hosted by a provider. A prompt is the text I send. A completion is what comes back. Inference is running the trained model; training is building it (done by the provider, costs millions). I only do inference, through an HTTPS API.

Loop at runtime:

prompt tokens -> model -> probabilities for next token -> pick one -> append
      ^                                                              |
      +--------------------- repeat until stop token ----------------+

Training has two stages: pre-training (read huge text, learn language and facts) and post-training (instruction tuning, RLHF) which makes it behave like an assistant. As an app developer I do neither.

Good at: summarising, rewriting, extraction, classification, explaining code, Q&A over text I provide. Weak at: exact arithmetic, today's news, my private data, guaranteed factual accuracy. Hallucination means fluent, confident, wrong output; it happens because the objective is "plausible continuation", not "true statement". Fixes live around the model (give it the source text, use tools, validate output).

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a, this is a mental-model question; the first-API-call question shows the code.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "The model looks up the answer in a database."
  • Confusing training with inference, or thinking my API calls train the model (by default they do not; check the provider data policy).
  • Treating hallucination as a bug that will be fixed rather than a property to design around.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does it hallucinate? → It optimises for plausible next tokens, not truth, and has no built-in way to say "I never saw this".
  2. Pre-training vs post-training? → Pre-training learns language and facts from raw text; post-training shapes behaviour into a helpful assistant.
  3. How do you reduce hallucination in an app? → Supply the source text in the prompt (RAG), allow tools, ask for citations, validate outputs, and let it say "I don't know".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it is a smart chatbot trained on the internet." Senior: next-token prediction, stateless inference, hallucination as a design constraint, and what the app must add (grounding, validation).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support bot confidently quoted a refund policy that did not exist; the fix was injecting the real policy text into the prompt and requiring it to answer only from that text.

questions.promptHtml: People say LLM APIs are "stateless". What does that mean, and what does it force me to do in my code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The single most common beginner misconception is that the model remembers the chat. This tells me whether you will build chat features correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stateless means the model keeps nothing between requests. Each call is independent, so my code must send everything the model needs (system prompt, earlier turns, documents) every single time. A "conversation" is a list my application stores and resends.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When I call the API, the server loads the model, reads my request tokens, generates, returns, and forgets. There is no session on the model side. If turn 1 says "My name is Asha" and turn 2 sends only "What is my name?", the model has no way to know.

turn 2 request: [ user: "My name is Asha", assistant: "Hi Asha", user: "What is my name?" ]
                  ^ my app re-sends the earlier turns every call

Consequences:

  1. Cost and latency grow with history, since all of it is re-processed and billed as input tokens each turn.
  2. I own storage: memory for a demo, a database or Redis keyed by conversation id in production.
  3. I own trimming: window, summary or token budget, else I eventually hit the context limit.
  4. Isolation: one user's history must never leak into another's request.

Some vendors offer provider-side stateful conversation features; know which one you are using, because then retention and billing rules differ.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a, the multi-turn question has the three-language history example.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sending only the latest user message and wondering why context is lost.
  • A global history list shared by all users in a server.
  • Forgetting that resending history is re-billed every turn.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you store history? → DB or Redis keyed by conversation id; memory only for demos.
  2. How does ChatGPT seem to remember across chats? → Separate stored "memory" facts injected into the prompt, not model weights.
  3. What if the history does not fit? → Sliding window, summarise old turns, or retrieve relevant past facts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "you have to send the history." Senior adds the cost curve, storage and isolation design, and trimming without breaking role order or dropping the system prompt.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A multi-tenant bot stored history in a module-level list; users saw fragments of each other's chats until history was keyed by conversation id.

questions.promptHtml: What is a token, why does the API bill in tokens instead of words, and how do I estimate or measure token counts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cost, latency and limits are all in tokens. A developer who thinks in words will mis-budget.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A token is the unit of text a model reads and writes: a whole common word, part of a word, a character or punctuation. In English it is about 4 characters or 0.75 words, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words. I pay per input and output token, and I measure with the provider's token-counting endpoint or the usage field, not by guessing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A tokenizer splits text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary, so "unbelievable" may become "un", "believ", "able". Models operate on these pieces' ids, never raw letters. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so counts differ across models.

Why it matters:

  1. Cost: price per million input tokens and (usually higher) per million output tokens. Prices change; look them up ("verify").
  2. Latency: output is produced one token at a time, so 1,000 output tokens take roughly ten times as long as 100.
  3. Limits: the context window and max output are in tokens.

Hindi, Chinese, Arabic and code usually use more tokens per word, so a Hindi support bot can cost noticeably more than an English one for the same meaning. Measure with real samples.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How many tokens is this sentence?"}],
)
print(count.input_tokens)  # an integer such as 14
// Java SDK from Kotlin; verify method names for your SDK version
val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()
val params = MessageCountTokensParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
    .addUserMessage("How many tokens is this sentence?")
    .build()
println(client.messages().countTokens(params).inputTokens())
AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv();
MessageCountTokensParams params = MessageCountTokensParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")
    .addUserMessage("How many tokens is this sentence?")
    .build();
System.out.println(client.messages().countTokens(params).inputTokens()); // verify names in SDK docs

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "1 token = 1 word."
  • Using character math in production instead of the counter or the usage field.
  • Assuming the same text has the same count across different models.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are output tokens pricier? → Generating is sequential and compute-heavy compared with reading the prompt in parallel.
  2. Why do non-English texts cost more? → The tokenizer vocabulary is dominated by English, so other scripts split into more pieces.
  3. How would you budget before sending? → Count tokens first, compare against the window minus the reply I want, trim if over.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "about 4 characters per token." Senior: knows tokenizers differ per model, language skews counts, and logs actual usage instead of estimating.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Average tokens per request jumped 8x after someone pasted a full PDF into the prompt; a dashboard on input tokens per request caught it.

questions.promptHtml: What is a context window, and does it include the model's answer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many beginners forget the output shares the window, then hit truncation or errors with a near-full prompt.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one request, and it counts both my input (system prompt, history, documents) and the output it generates. If I send 150,000 tokens into a 200,000 window, only about 50,000 remain for the reply. Exceed it and the API returns an error, so I must trim or summarise.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
|<-------------- context window (e.g. 200k) -------------->|
| system | history | documents | question |  reply (output) |
|<------------ input tokens ---------->|<-- output tokens -->|

A separate cap, max output tokens, limits a single reply and is usually smaller than the window. Window sizes have grown a lot, but exact numbers per model are fast-moving ("verify" in model docs).

A bigger window is not free: cost and latency scale with input size, and models can miss details buried in the middle of very long inputs. So I still select what goes in (retrieval, trimming) instead of dumping everything.

When I exceed the limit: typically a 400 invalid-request error. My code should count tokens before sending and apply a policy: drop oldest turns, summarise, or retrieve only relevant chunks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a here; the token-counting snippet in the tokens question shows the pre-check.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the output counts, so a full prompt leaves no room to answer.
  • Assuming a larger window always improves answers.
  • Setting max_tokens above what the remaining window can hold.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Window vs max output tokens? → Window is the total budget for the request; max output caps just the reply.
  2. What happens past the limit? → Usually a 400 error; some UIs silently drop old messages.
  3. Is long context a replacement for retrieval? → No: higher cost, slower, and recall can degrade; retrieval keeps prompts small and relevant.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it is the max input size." Senior: input plus output, budgets the reply explicitly, and treats long context as a cost/latency trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A summarisation job passed documents near the window limit and returned half-sentences; the room left for output was a few hundred tokens.

questions.promptHtml: What are the system, user and assistant roles in a chat API, and where does the system prompt go?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can shape a request correctly and know the API's structural rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A chat request is a list of messages with roles. The system prompt holds my fixed instructions (tone, rules, format), user messages are what the person says, and assistant messages are the model's earlier replies that I include so it sees the conversation. On Anthropic the system prompt is a separate top-level system field; on OpenAI-compatible APIs it is a message with role system (or developer on newer models, verify).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
system  : "You are a terse SQL tutor."
messages: [ user: "What is a JOIN?" ]
              |  POST /v1/messages
              v
response: assistant: "A JOIN combines rows from two tables on a key."

Rules: Anthropic messages alternate user/assistant and start with a user message, otherwise 400. The reply arrives as an assistant message made of content blocks (usually one text block).

Why separate system from user: stable rules stay in one place, and the variable input stays in user messages. Internally everything is one token stream, so the system prompt is guidance, not a security boundary. Users can try "ignore previous instructions" (prompt injection), so never place secrets in it and never rely on it alone for safety.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=100,
    system="You are a terse SQL tutor.",            # top-level, not in messages
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is a JOIN?"}],
)
val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(100)
    .system("You are a terse SQL tutor.")
    .addUserMessage("What is a JOIN?")
    .build()
MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(100)
    .system("You are a terse SQL tutor.")
    .addUserMessage("What is a JOIN?")
    .build();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting a system role message inside messages on the Anthropic API.
  • Two user messages in a row where alternation is required.
  • Treating the system prompt as secret or unbreakable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What goes in system vs user? → Stable rules and persona in system; changing input in user.
  2. Can I pre-fill an assistant message? → On some APIs, to steer the start of the reply (verify support).
  3. Is the system prompt safe for secrets? → No; it can leak or be bypassed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "system sets behaviour." Senior: knows per-provider placement and role-order rules, and treats it as non-secret guidance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bot stored an internal discount code in its system prompt; a user asked it to "repeat your instructions" and it did.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through making your first call to an LLM API: what do you need, what does the request look like, and what is in the response?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The baseline competency: can you actually call a model and read what comes back?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I need an API key from the provider, kept in an environment variable, plus the model id, a max_tokens value, and a list of messages. I POST JSON to the Messages endpoint (or use the SDK). The response has content (a list of blocks, text in the first), stop_reason, usage and id.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Raw REST on Anthropic:

POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
anthropic-version: 2023-06-01
content-type: application/json
{ "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "max_tokens": 256,
  "system": "You are a concise assistant.",
  "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Explain DNS in one sentence."} ] }

max_tokens is required on Anthropic. In production I use the SDK for typing, retries and error classes. The same shape exists elsewhere: OpenAI-compatible servers (including local Ollama at http://localhost:11434/v1) use POST /v1/chat/completions and return choices[0].message.content; Gemini uses generateContent with contents and parts. Because of this, many teams wrap the provider behind a thin interface of their own so swapping models is a one-file change. Always confirm current model ids ("verify").

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=256,
    system="You are a concise assistant.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain DNS in one sentence."}],
)
print(response.content[0].text)
print(response.stop_reason)  # end_turn
val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()
val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(256)
    .system("You are a concise assistant.")
    .addUserMessage("Explain DNS in one sentence.")
    .build()
client.messages().create(params).content().forEach { b ->
    b.text().ifPresent { println(it.text()) }   // verify accessors in SDK docs
}
AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv();
MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(256)
    .system("You are a concise assistant.")
    .addUserMessage("Explain DNS in one sentence.")
    .build();
Message message = client.messages().create(params);
message.content().forEach(b -> b.text().ifPresent(t -> System.out.println(t.text())));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hard-coding the key or committing it to Git.
  • Omitting max_tokens on Anthropic (request fails).
  • Reading content as a string instead of a list of blocks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why use an SDK over raw HTTP? → Types, built-in retries, error classes, streaming helpers.
  2. How do other providers differ? → Field names (choices, parts), concepts are the same.
  3. Can a mobile app call this directly? → No; the key would ship in the APK. Call your own backend.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: makes the call and prints text. Senior: reads stop_reason and usage, keeps the key server-side, and hides the provider behind an interface.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leaked key committed to a public repo was abused within hours; the key was rotated and moved to a secrets manager.

questions.promptHtml: What do temperature, max_tokens and stop sequences do, and how would you pick values for an extraction task versus a brainstorming task?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you understand sampling at a practical level and know the failure modes of each knob.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: At each step the model gives a probability for every possible next token and sampling picks one. Temperature controls randomness: near 0 it picks the most likely token (focused), higher gives variety. max_tokens is a hard cap on reply length, and a stop sequence ends generation when that text appears. For extraction I use low temperature and a tight cap; for brainstorming I raise temperature.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parameter Effect Use
max_tokens Cuts output at N tokens (stop_reason = max_tokens) Always set
temperature Randomness Low for extraction/code, higher for ideas
top_p Sample from smallest token set with cumulative probability p Alternative to temperature; change one, not both
stop_sequences Ends generation at given strings (not returned) Cut at a tag or "\n\nUser:"

Caveats: temperature 0 is nearly but not guaranteed deterministic, so I never write logic needing bit-exact repeats. Some newer reasoning models restrict sampling parameters ("verify" in docs). High temperature does not make the model smarter; it raises the risk of odd tokens. If answers are bad, fix the prompt first.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=100, temperature=0.2,
    stop_sequences=["\n\n"],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name three Android lifecycle callbacks."}],
)
print(r.stop_reason)  # end_turn, max_tokens or stop_sequence
val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(100).temperature(0.2)
    .addStopSequence("\n\n")
    .addUserMessage("Name three Android lifecycle callbacks.")
    .build()
println(client.messages().create(params).stopReason())
MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(100).temperature(0.2)
    .addStopSequence("\n\n")
    .addUserMessage("Name three Android lifecycle callbacks.")
    .build();
System.out.println(client.messages().create(params).stopReason()); // verify accessor

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Temperature 0 is fully deterministic."
  • Tuning temperature and top_p aggressively together.
  • Ignoring stop_reason == max_tokens.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. top_p vs temperature? → Top_p truncates the candidate set; temperature reshapes the whole distribution. Change one.
  2. Why might the same prompt give different answers at temperature 0? → Hosted systems can have tiny numeric differences.
  3. Does a lower max_tokens make the model concise? → No, it just cuts it off; ask for brevity in the prompt.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "temperature is creativity." Senior: explains the distribution, pairs max_tokens with stop_reason checks, and does not assume determinism.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An intent classifier at temperature 1.0 flipped labels between runs; setting 0 and validating against an allowed label list stabilised it.

questions.contextHtml:
An invoice-extraction feature asks the model for JSON with vendor, date and 40 line items. In production about 6 percent of requests fail with JSONDecodeError: Unterminated string at char 1021. Average output is around 900 tokens. The code:

r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=256, temperature=0,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Extract invoice as JSON:\n{text}"}],
)
data = json.loads(r.content[0].text)

Short invoices work fine; invoices with many line items fail. No 4xx or 5xx errors appear in the logs.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model is unreliable at JSON, lower the temperature or retry." Temperature is already 0, retries repeat the same truncation, and it ignores the response metadata.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do failing requests share a property (long invoices)? What is stop_reason on failures? What is usage.output_tokens on failures (does it equal 256)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise max_tokens to a safe ceiling (for example 2,048) and treat stop_reason == "max_tokens" as a failure, not data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) output cut by max_tokens; (b) model wrapped JSON in prose; (c) invalid escape in a string; (d) a proxy truncating the body.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log stop_reason and usage.output_tokens for failures. If it is max_tokens with output_tokens exactly 256, hypothesis (a) is confirmed. Compare failing invoice sizes with passing ones.
  5. Root cause: A cap of 256 tokens is far below the needed ~900; the model was cut mid-string, so the JSON is invalid. A 200 status says nothing about completeness.
  6. Fix: Short term, raise the cap and add the stop-reason check. Long term, estimate needed output from the input size, or split long invoices into chunks, and use structured-output features (later topic).
  7. Prevention: Alert on the rate of stop_reason == max_tokens; a test with a 100-line invoice.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not retry blindly with the same cap, and not set an enormous cap everywhere (cost and latency ceilings matter).
if r.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
    raise ValueError("output truncated; raise max_tokens or chunk the input")
data = json.loads(r.content[0].text)
val msg = client.messages().create(params)
check(msg.stopReason().toString() != "max_tokens") { "output truncated" } // verify enum compare in SDK
Message msg = client.messages().create(params);
if (msg.stopReason().toString().contains("max_tokens")) {   // verify enum compare in SDK
    throw new IllegalStateException("output truncated");
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if even the max cap is not enough? → Chunk the invoice, extract per chunk, merge.
  • Could streaming fix it? → No, truncation is the cap, not the transport.
  • How do you detect refusals the same way? → Check stop_reason and validate the schema.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team debugged "flaky JSON" for a week, tuning prompts. The log of stop_reason showed every failure was max_tokens; one config value fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the model, retries, lowers temperature.
  • Hire: spots max_tokens truncation and checks stop_reason.
  • Strong hire: adds stop-reason alerting, sizing logic, chunking, and validates parsed output.

questions.promptHtml: How do you compute the cost of a request, and what should you log on every call?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cost control is a core production concern; interviewers want to see you instrument it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each response has a usage object with input and output token counts. Cost is input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price, where output is usually several times pricier. I log both counts, the model id and the request id for every call, and keep prices in config because they change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
cost = input_tokens * price_in_per_token + output_tokens * price_out_per_token

Fields to read each time: content, stop_reason, usage.input_tokens, usage.output_tokens, id (and the request-id header), model. With prompt caching the usage also shows cache creation and cache read tokens (production topic).

Why log the request id: to report issues to the provider. Why log the model: aliases and routing can change what served you.

Cost levers: shorter prompts, a cheaper model for easy tasks, lower max_tokens, prompt caching, batch APIs for non-urgent work, response caching. Remember that a chat resends history each turn, so cost per turn rises as it grows.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
u = response.usage
print(u.input_tokens, u.output_tokens)
# placeholder prices per million tokens; load real ones from config (verify)
cost = u.input_tokens * 3 / 1_000_000 + u.output_tokens * 15 / 1_000_000
val usage = message.usage()
// placeholder prices per million tokens; load from config (verify)
val cost = usage.inputTokens() * 3.0 / 1_000_000 + usage.outputTokens() * 15.0 / 1_000_000
Usage usage = message.usage(); // com.anthropic.models.messages.Usage
// placeholder prices per million tokens; load from config (verify)
double cost = usage.inputTokens() * 3.0 / 1_000_000 + usage.outputTokens() * 15.0 / 1_000_000;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Estimating cost from word counts.
  • Hard-coding prices in source.
  • Not logging usage and request id, so a bill or support ticket cannot be debugged.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Worked example? → 1,000 input and 500 output tokens at $3 and $15 per million: 0.003 + 0.0075 = $0.0105.
  2. How do you cap a free tier? → Per-user token ledger checked before the call.
  3. What alert would you set? → Average input tokens per request, and spend per feature per hour.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: reads the pricing page. Senior: per-request logging, per-feature attribution, budgets/alerts, and cost levers ranked by impact.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature costing $400/day was invisible until usage was tagged by feature; one prompt template was shipping a 30k-token boilerplate.

questions.promptHtml: Which HTTP error codes can an LLM API return and which should I retry?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Retrying the wrong errors wastes money and hides bugs; not retrying the right ones hurts reliability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: 4xx errors are my fault and should not be retried: 400 bad request, 401 bad key, 403 no permission, 404 unknown model, 413 too large. The exceptions are 429 (rate limited) and 5xx or overloaded responses (500, 503, Anthropic's 529), which are transient and should be retried with backoff. Timeouts and connection errors are also retried.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Status Meaning Action
400 Invalid request (bad JSON, missing max_tokens, over the window, bad role order) Fix the request
401 Missing or wrong key Fix key/header
403 No permission Fix permissions or model access
404 Unknown model/endpoint Fix model id
413 Body too large Shrink
429 Rate limit Back off, honour retry-after
500/503/529 Provider error or overload Retry, then fall back

A 200 does not guarantee a usable answer: it may be truncated (max_tokens), refused, or in the wrong format. I validate the content too. Mid-stream errors arrive after a 200 has already been sent.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=3, timeout=60.0)
try:
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=200,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])
except anthropic.RateLimitError:        # 429, SDK retries exhausted
    print("slow down")
except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:   # other 4xx/5xx
    print(e.status_code, e.message)
except anthropic.APIConnectionError:
    print("network problem")
val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.builder().fromEnv().maxRetries(3).build() // verify options
try {
    println(client.messages().create(params).content())
} catch (e: RateLimitException) {
    println("slow down")
} catch (e: AnthropicException) {
    println("API error: ${e.message}")
}
AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.builder().fromEnv().maxRetries(3).build();
try {
    System.out.println(client.messages().create(params).content());
} catch (RateLimitException e) {
    System.out.println("slow down");
} catch (AnthropicException e) {
    System.out.println("API error: " + e.getMessage());
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying 400/401 in a loop.
  • Treating any 200 as success.
  • No explicit timeout, so a hung request blocks a thread or UI.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 400 on a long chat? → Probably over the context window; trim history.
  2. 529 vs 429? → 529 means provider overloaded; 429 means my own limits.
  3. Do SDKs retry for me? → Usually a small default number; verify and configure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "retry on errors." Senior: classifies by code, honours retry-after, sets timeouts, validates 200 bodies, and defines fallbacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job retried a 401 every second for a day after a key rotation, burning rate limit and flooding logs.

questions.promptHtml: What is exponential backoff with jitter, and why is plain fixed-interval retry dangerous during an outage?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Retry storms turn a small provider blip into your own outage; this is a standard reliability question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure (about 1 s, 2 s, 4 s) up to a max number of attempts. Jitter adds a random amount to each wait so thousands of clients do not retry in lockstep. Fixed fast retries multiply the load on an already struggling service and keep my own clients rate-limited.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Suppose 1,000 requests fail at the same second. With a fixed 1 s retry, all 1,000 hit again together, fail again, and so on: a retry storm. With backoff they spread out in time; with jitter (for example "full jitter": wait a random value between 0 and the current cap) they spread within each window too.

Rules: only retry transient errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), cap attempts (3 to 5) and total elapsed time, honour retry-after when present, and make the operation safe to repeat. Retrying the LLM call is safe because it only reads; but retrying a tool that sends an email is not, unless it has an idempotency key.
