sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import random, time
def with_retry(fn, attempts=4):
    for i in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except (anthropic.RateLimitError, anthropic.APIConnectionError, anthropic.InternalServerError):
            if i == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 2 ** i))   # full jitter: 0..1, 0..2, 0..4 s
fun <T> withRetry(attempts: Int = 4, fn: () -> T): T {
    for (i in 0 until attempts) {
        try { return fn() } catch (e: RateLimitException) {
            if (i == attempts - 1) throw e
            Thread.sleep((Math.random() * (1L shl i) * 1000).toLong()) // full jitter
        }
    }
    error("unreachable")
}
static <T> T withRetry(int attempts, Supplier<T> fn) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int i = 0; ; i++) {
        try { return fn.get(); }
        catch (RateLimitException e) {
            if (i == attempts - 1) throw e;
            Thread.sleep((long) (Math.random() * (1L << i) * 1000)); // full jitter
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying every error type.
  • Retrying without a cap, or without jitter.
  • Retrying at every layer (SDK, service, gateway), multiplying attempts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not retry forever? → Unbounded latency and load; fail fast, fall back or queue.
  2. Retries at multiple layers? → 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls per user action; retry at one layer only.
  3. What if the provider is down for 20 minutes? → Circuit breaker plus fallback model or friendly degraded message.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "retry three times." Senior: jitter, caps, retry-after, idempotency, one retry layer, and a circuit breaker.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An 8-minute provider incident became a 40-minute one for a team because every worker retried every second until its own queue was saturated.

questions.promptHtml: How does streaming work for LLM APIs, and what does it actually improve?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Streaming is in nearly every chat UI; interviewers want to see you understand the protocol and its failure modes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With streaming, the server keeps one HTTP response open and sends small Server-Sent Events as tokens are generated, instead of one body at the end. It does not make the model faster overall; it improves perceived latency because the user sees text after the time to first token (TTFT). The catch is that errors can arrive mid-stream after a 200 was already sent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
I enable it with "stream": true. The response is Content-Type: text/event-stream; each event has event: and data: lines. Anthropic's order:

message_start          -> metadata, input usage
content_block_start
content_block_delta    -> {"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":"Hel"}}  (many)
content_block_stop
message_delta          -> stop_reason, final output usage
message_stop
(ping events; "error" events can appear mid-stream)

OpenAI-compatible APIs stream data: {...} chunks with choices[0].delta.content and end with data: [DONE]. SDKs hide the parsing.

Gotchas: partial text on dropped connections, proxies buffering the response (nginx needs X-Accel-Buffering: no), JSON cannot be parsed until complete, and final usage arrives in the last events.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about Gradle."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
    final = stream.get_final_message()
print(final.usage.output_tokens)
// verify class names in the SDK docs
client.messages().createStreaming(params).use { resp ->
    resp.stream().forEach { ev ->
        ev.contentBlockDelta().ifPresent { d -> d.delta().text().ifPresent { print(it.text()) } }
    }
}
try (StreamResponse<RawMessageStreamEvent> resp = client.messages().createStreaming(params)) {
    resp.stream().forEach(ev -> ev.contentBlockDelta().ifPresent(
        d -> d.delta().text().ifPresent(t -> System.out.print(t.text()))));
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying streaming makes generation faster.
  • Assuming 200 means the stream completed.
  • Logging usage from the first event instead of the last.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is TTFT? → Time to first token; the metric users feel.
  2. How do you stream to a phone? → My backend streams SSE; the app exposes it as a Kotlin Flow (later topic).
  3. How do you handle a drop mid-answer? → Keep the partial text, mark it incomplete, and offer retry or continue.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "tokens arrive as they are generated." Senior: knows the event sequence, perceived vs real latency, buffering and mid-stream error handling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Streaming worked locally but users saw one delayed block in production because the reverse proxy buffered responses.

questions.contextHtml:
A Spring/Flask-style backend serves a support chatbot to about 300 concurrent users. QA reports that "sometimes the bot mentions another customer's order number" and that after long chats the API returns 400s. The code:

history = []   # module level

def chat(user_text):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
                               system="You are a support agent.", messages=history)
    reply = r.content[0].text
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

Log excerpt: 400 invalid_request_error: prompt is too long for one user after about 140 turns. Average message is 120 tokens.
questions.promptHtml: Identify every bug and propose a fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a try/except around the call." That hides the data leak and the cause of the 400.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the server multi-threaded or multi-process? Where does conversation id come from? What is the window of the model?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Treat the leak as a privacy incident: disable the feature or deploy a per-conversation store quickly, rotate nothing yet but notify security.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one global list shared across users; (b) no trimming, so history exceeds the window (140 turns x 2 x 120 = about 33,600 tokens plus others, on a shared list far higher); (c) failed calls leave a dangling user message; (d) the system prompt is fine.
  4. How I'd verify each: Two test clients chatting at once, assert histories are separate; log usage.input_tokens per call; simulate an error and inspect the list.
  5. Root cause: A shared mutable global list mixes all users' turns (leak and runaway growth), and nothing bounds it.
  6. Fix: Key history by conversation id in Redis/DB, load per request, trim, append only after success.
  7. Prevention: Concurrency test for isolation, alert on input tokens per request, cap conversation length.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise limits; unbounded history is also a cost problem.
def chat(conv_id, user_text):
    h = store.load(conv_id)
    msgs = (h + [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}])[-20:]   # sliding window
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
                               system="You are a support agent.", messages=msgs)
    reply = r.content[0].text
    store.save(conv_id, h + [{"role": "user", "content": user_text},
                             {"role": "assistant", "content": reply}])
    return reply
fun chat(convId: String, userText: String): String {
    val h = store.load(convId)                          // per-conversation list
    val msgs = (h + userMsg(userText)).takeLast(20)
    val reply = callModel(msgs)
    store.save(convId, h + userMsg(userText) + assistantMsg(reply))
    return reply
}
String chat(String convId, String userText) {
    List<MessageParam> h = store.load(convId);          // per-conversation list
    List<MessageParam> msgs = new ArrayList<>(h);
    msgs.add(userMsg(userText));
    List<MessageParam> window = msgs.subList(Math.max(0, msgs.size() - 20), msgs.size());
    String reply = callModel(window);
    msgs.add(assistantMsg(reply));
    store.save(convId, msgs);
    return reply;
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A window of 20 starts with an assistant message; what happens? → Role-order 400 on some APIs; trim to start at a user message.
  • What if users need long memory? → Summarise old turns into a note, keep the note plus recent turns.
  • Where must authorization happen? → On the server: verify the conversation id belongs to the caller.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A prototype shared a list across requests; it passed single-user tests for weeks. The first load test surfaced cross-user leakage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wraps in try/except.
  • Hire: finds the shared global and the missing trimming.
  • Strong hire: also handles failure atomicity, authorization, role-order after trimming and the incident response.

questions.promptHtml: Compare sliding window, summarisation and token-budget trimming for chat history. When would you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every chat product must bound history; the trade-offs show practical judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A sliding window keeps the last N turns: simple, but forgets early facts. Summarisation compresses old turns into a short note with a model call: keeps gist, costs an extra call and can lose detail. A token budget drops the oldest turns until the total fits under a limit: predictable cost. In practice I combine them: always keep the system prompt, a summary, and recent turns under a token budget.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy Pros Cons
Sliding window (last N) Trivial, deterministic Loses early facts; N turns can still be huge
Token budget Bounds cost and window Needs token counting
Summarisation Keeps long-range gist Extra latency and cost; may drop details or add errors
Retrieval / memory Scales to months of history More moving parts (later topics)

Rules whichever I choose: keep the system prompt every call, keep user/assistant alternation (do not start the window with an assistant message), leave room for the reply, and never cut a tool-call pair in half (later topic). Store the full transcript separately from what I send.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def trim(history, budget_tokens, count):
    while history and count(history) > budget_tokens:
        history = history[2:]           # drop oldest user+assistant pair
    return history
fun trim(history: List<MessageParam>, budget: Int, count: (List<MessageParam>) -> Int): List<MessageParam> {
    var h = history
    while (h.size >= 2 && count(h) > budget) h = h.drop(2)  // drop oldest pair
    return h
}
static List<MessageParam> trim(List<MessageParam> history, int budget, ToIntFunction<List<MessageParam>> count) {
    List<MessageParam> h = new ArrayList<>(history);
    while (h.size() >= 2 && count.applyAsInt(h) > budget) h = new ArrayList<>(h.subList(2, h.size()));
    return h;
}

questions.promptHtml: How would you choose between a small, a balanced and a large model for a new feature?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you decide with data and constraints rather than defaulting to the biggest model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I write down what "good" means, build about 50 real examples, start with the balanced tier, then try the small tier to save cost and latency, moving up only if quality falls short. I also check context window, latency, cost at expected volume, modality and tool support, privacy terms and rate limits. Often the best design uses several models: a small one for easy or routing steps and a large one for hard cases.

Providers ship a ladder (for Anthropic, verify current lineup: claude-haiku-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-opus-5-5, plus claude-fable-5-1 in this course's notes). Open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) can run on my own hardware with Ollama or vLLM.

Need Lean towards
Cheap, fast, high volume (classify, extract) Small tier
General features, coding, summarising Balanced tier
Hard reasoning, long agentic tasks Largest tier
Data cannot leave my network Self-hosted open model
Offline on a phone On-device model

Decision steps: define task and metric, test on my own data (not leaderboards), compare cost per request at volume, check latency targets, check hard constraints (window, modalities, privacy, availability), then pin the model id and re-run the test set before upgrading.

questions.contextHtml: A chat UI streams answers using SSE. In staging, text appears word by word with TTFT around 600 ms. After release behind a corporate load balancer plus nginx, users report "the page freezes for 8 to 15 seconds, then the whole answer appears at once". Backend logs show tokens being written within 1 second. Status codes are all 200. About 5 percent of users also see answers cut off mid-sentence with no error message. Average answer: 400 tokens.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose both symptoms and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model is slow in production." The backend logs prove tokens leave within 1 second, so the delay is downstream.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does curl -N straight to the app server stream? Is compression enabled on the proxy? Do cut-offs correlate with long answers or a specific network/timeout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Bypass or reconfigure the proxy for the stream route.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) nginx/LB buffering the response; (b) gzip middleware buffering until a size threshold; (c) idle or max-duration timeout cutting connections (cut-offs); (d) an error event mid-stream being dropped by the UI.
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -N against app, then against the LB, compare arrival timing; inspect response headers; reproduce a long answer and watch for the connection close time; check the client handles the SSE error event.
  5. Root cause: Proxy buffering turns many small events into one block; a proxy timeout (or an upstream error after the 200) truncates the stream without any status change.
  6. Fix: Disable buffering for that route (X-Accel-Buffering: no, proxy_buffering off), disable gzip for text/event-stream, raise proxy read timeouts, send periodic keepalive pings, and make the client surface "incomplete answer" with a retry/continue.
  7. Prevention: Integration test through the real proxy chain measuring TTFT; synthetic probe in monitoring.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove streaming; I would not rely on status codes to detect success.

questions.promptHtml: Can I rely on an LLM returning the same output for the same input? What should I design around instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand non-determinism and can design robust systems around it, including tests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. Sampling is random by design, and even at temperature 0 hosted systems can vary slightly, so I never depend on bit-exact repeats. Instead I constrain outputs (formats, allowed labels, schemas), validate them, set low temperature where consistency matters, and test with evaluation sets that measure pass rates rather than exact string equality.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sources of variation: sampling randomness, batching and floating-point effects on the provider, and model updates behind an alias. Some providers offer a seed for best-effort reproducibility; do not assume equivalent guarantees on every API (verify).

Design implications:

  1. Validate: parse and check outputs; reject or retry invalid ones.
  2. Constrain: ask for a fixed label set or a JSON schema (later topic).
  3. Test statistically: run each case several times and require a pass rate (for example 95 percent), not equality.
  4. Cache if repeatability matters: store the first accepted result for a given input.
  5. Pin model id so behaviour does not change underneath me.

A fake client in unit tests returns fixed text, so tests of my own code are deterministic; evals of the model are separate and statistical.

  3. Does a seed fix it? → Only best-effort where offered; verify per provider.

questions.contextHtml: A nightly job summarises 20,000 tickets using 50 worker threads. Each worker retries failures immediately up to 10 times. Your org limit is 400 requests per minute (example numbers). At 02:00 the job starts; logs show 429 rate_limit_error for most calls, the job takes 6 hours instead of the expected 55 minutes, and the interactive chat feature that shares the same key starts failing at 02:10. Provider status is green.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and redesign the job.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Ask the provider for a higher limit." That may help later but does not explain the slowdown or the impact on the live feature.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the limit per key/org and shared with chat? Is it requests/min or tokens/min? Does the job need to finish by a deadline? Do 429 responses include retry-after?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause or throttle the batch job to protect the interactive feature.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 50 workers with no pacing exceed 400 RPM; (b) immediate retries amplify the load (retry storm); (c) shared key starves chat; (d) provider outage (ruled out by status).
  4. How I'd verify each: Count requests per minute from logs including retries; check 429 headers; look at per-workload request counts.
  5. Root cause: Burst concurrency plus zero-delay retries keep the client permanently over the limit, and the same key means the batch steals capacity from chat.
  6. Fix: Token-bucket rate limiter at about 80 percent of the limit (320 RPM), exponential backoff with jitter, honour retry-after; separate keys or quotas for batch vs interactive; consider the provider's batch API for non-urgent work. 20,000 / 320 per minute is about 62 minutes.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of 429 rate and RPM per workload; load test before launching.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add more workers (more contention) or retry forever.

        time.sleep(60 / 320 * 5)     # crude pacing; use a real token bucket in production
        return summarise(item)

sections.html:
• Limit is in tokens per minute, not requests? → Throttle by estimated tokens; smaller prompts help.
  • Deadline moves to 20 minutes? → Higher tier or multiple provider accounts, or a cheaper model with higher limits.
  • Job fails halfway? → Idempotent per-ticket processing with a done-marker so reruns skip finished items.

sections.html: A "quick" backfill using the production key took down the live assistant for 40 minutes; separate keys per workload became policy.

sections.html:
• No hire: asks for higher limits only.
  • Hire: adds backoff, jitter and throttling.
  • Strong hire: separates workloads, computes the throughput maths, adds resumability and monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A tutoring chat app sends full history every turn. Average message is 150 tokens, reply 250 tokens. Sessions average 30 turns today, 50,000 sessions per month, on a model priced (example) at $3 per million input and $15 per million output tokens. Marketing plans a campaign to reach 500,000 sessions per month, and product wants sessions up to 60 turns. Finance asks for a forecast and a plan.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate the cost shape, explain why it grows faster than linearly per session, and propose reductions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cost is per token so 10x users is 10x cost." That ignores that per-session cost is quadratic in turns.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the system prompt large? Is caching available? What quality loss is acceptable from trimming? What is the p95 session length?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap history to a token budget before the campaign.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Input tokens dominate because history is resent each turn.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute from logs: input tokens at turn k.
  5. Root cause: At turn k the input is about k x 400 tokens (150 + 250 per turn). Total input over n turns is 400 x n(n+1)/2. For n = 30: 400 x 465 = 186,000 input tokens; output is 30 x 250 = 7,500. For n = 60: 400 x 1,830 = 732,000 input, about 3.9x for 2x the turns. Cost per session at 30 turns: 186,000 x $3/1M = $0.558 plus 7,500 x $15/1M = $0.113, about $0.67; so 50,000 sessions = about $33.5k/month; 500,000 sessions at 30 turns = about $335k; at 60 turns: 732,000 x $3/1M = $2.20 plus 15,000 x $15/1M = $0.225, about $2.42 per session, so about $1.2M/month.
  6. Fix: Sliding window or token budget (keep, say, last 10 turns: input per turn capped near 4,000 tokens), summary of older turns, prompt caching for the stable prefix (verify pricing), smaller model for simple turns. A 4,000 token cap at 30 turns is 120,000 input or less, roughly 35 percent saving, and it flattens growth to linear.
  7. Prevention: Per-session cost metric, alert on p95 tokens per session, force "new chat" prompts after N turns.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Summaries can lose details, so I keep a pinned facts list; I would not remove history entirely.
def cost(turns, msg=150, rep=250, pin=3.0, pout=15.0):
    inp = sum(k * (msg + rep) for k in range(1, turns + 1))   # history grows each turn
    return inp * pin / 1e6 + turns * rep * pout / 1e6
print(cost(30), cost(60))   # about 0.67 and 2.42
fun cost(turns: Int, msg: Int = 150, rep: Int = 250, pin: Double = 3.0, pout: Double = 15.0): Double {
    val inp = (1..turns).sumOf { it * (msg + rep).toLong() }
    return inp * pin / 1e6 + turns * rep * pout / 1e6
}
static double cost(int turns, int msg, int rep, double pin, double pout) {
    long inp = 0;
    for (int k = 1; k <= turns; k++) inp += (long) k * (msg + rep);
    return inp * pin / 1e6 + (double) turns * rep * pout / 1e6;
}

• Caching halves input price? → Only the stable prefix qualifies; savings depend on hit rate (verify specifics).
  • Quality complaints after trimming? → Retrieval of relevant earlier turns instead of recency.
  • Could a bigger window solve it? → No, it increases cost per turn.

sections.html: Early beta sessions were short, so costs looked fine; the long-session tail (5 percent of users) produced 40 percent of spend.

sections.html:
• No hire: linear scaling.

  • Strong hire: gives the maths, forecast, caching/routing options and quality guardrails.

questions.contextHtml: An assistant streams answers into a chat UI and also writes the final text to a database and charges the user's token quota from the first message_start event's input usage. During a provider overload, 3 percent of streams died after 100 to 300 tokens. Symptoms: the UI showed half answers with no error, the DB stored partial answers as "final", users were charged output they never saw, and a downstream summariser then trained on the partial text. HTTP status was 200 for all of them. Logs show event: error data: {"type":"error","error":{"type":"overloaded_error"}} in raw traces, but the app ignored it.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: causes, fixes and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We should retry on errors." The errors came after a 200, so status-based retry never ran.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the SDK raise on error events? Did we persist on stream end or on message_stop? What exactly does the quota charge on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mark messages stored in the incident window as incomplete; refund affected quota; pause the downstream job.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) error events not handled; (b) completion defined by stream close, not message_stop; (c) billing uses start-of-stream estimate; (d) UI has no incomplete state.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay raw traces; grep for error events; check code path on exceptions.
  5. Root cause: The app equated "HTTP 200 and stream ended" with success, so truncated output was persisted as complete.
  6. Fix: Treat the stream as complete only after message_stop with a stop_reason. On error or disconnect, store the text with status incomplete, show "interrupted, retry" in UI, and offer continue/regenerate. Charge from the final message_delta usage (and for failed streams, reconcile with what was delivered). Stop downstream consumers from reading incomplete rows.
  7. Prevention: Fault-injection test that kills a stream at token 50; state machine (streaming, complete, incomplete); alerts on incomplete-rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not silently auto-regenerate and append (confusing text, double cost); I would not hide partials entirely, since users value what was delivered.

questions.promptHtml: Why pin model ids in production, and how do you structure code so a model or provider swap is cheap and safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Model churn is constant; a senior engineer plans for deprecations, regressions and vendor risk.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Floating aliases can change behaviour without a deploy, so I pin an exact model id and move up deliberately after running my evaluation set. I put the provider behind a thin interface I own (one method taking messages and returning text plus usage), keep model ids and prices in config, and keep an eval set so I can compare a candidate model in minutes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reasons to pin: alias changes shift tone, format and accuracy; models get deprecated on a schedule, so I need to know which ids I use; prices and limits differ per id.

Structure:

app code -> LlmClient interface -> AnthropicAdapter | OpenAiCompatAdapter | FakeClient (tests)
                                     ^ model id, max_tokens, timeouts come from config

Upgrade procedure: new id in config -> run offline evals (50 to 200 real cases, pass-rate metric, cost and latency per request) -> shadow or canary a small percent of traffic -> roll out -> keep rollback one config change away.

Limit of abstraction: do not hide everything; features differ (tool use, caching, structured output). Abstract the common 80 percent and expose provider-specific options explicitly.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from typing import Protocol
class Llm(Protocol):
    def complete(self, system: str, messages: list[dict], max_tokens: int) -> tuple[str, dict]: ...

class AnthropicLlm:
    def __init__(self, model): self.client, self.model = anthropic.Anthropic(), model
    def complete(self, system, messages, max_tokens):
        r = self.client.messages.create(model=self.model, system=system, messages=messages, max_tokens=max_tokens)
        return r.content[0].text, {"in": r.usage.input_tokens, "out": r.usage.output_tokens}
interface Llm { fun complete(system: String, messages: List<Pair<String, String>>, maxTokens: Int): Pair<String, Usage> }
class FakeLlm(private val reply: String) : Llm {          // used in unit tests
    override fun complete(system: String, messages: List<Pair<String, String>>, maxTokens: Int) =
        reply to Usage(0, 0)
}
data class Usage(val input: Int, val output: Int)
interface Llm { Result complete(String system, List<Msg> messages, int maxTokens); }
record Msg(String role, String text) {}
record Result(String text, int in, int out) {}
class FakeLlm implements Llm {
    public Result complete(String system, List<Msg> messages, int maxTokens) { return new Result("ok", 0, 0); }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scattering model ids across the codebase.
  • Upgrading by changing the id without evals.
  • An abstraction so generic it removes useful provider features.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How handle a deprecation notice? → Run evals on the successor, canary, then switch before the cut-off date.
  2. How do you A/B models? → Route a percent by hash of user id and compare metrics.
  3. How avoid vendor lock-in? → Interface, portable prompts, OpenAI-compatible adapters, and regular cross-model eval runs.

questions.contextHtml: A startup's Android prototype calls the LLM API directly from the app with the key in BuildConfig. Beta has 2,000 users. After a blog post, the monthly bill goes from $200 to $7,800 in three days; a decompiled APK from a public forum thread shows the key. Product wants to keep "instant answers" and ship in two weeks. Backend team is two developers.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now, and what is the target architecture?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Obfuscate the key with ProGuard or hide it in native code." Anything shipped in the app can be extracted or sniffed from traffic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have user auth? Is the key scoped to a project with spend limits? What per-user usage is acceptable? Do we need streaming?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke and rotate the key now, set a hard spend limit and usage alerts on the provider project, ship a forced update or kill-switch for old builds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key extracted and used by third parties; (b) legitimate heavy use; (c) both. The provider's usage page by IP/time or request pattern separates them.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare usage logs to our user counts; check unfamiliar traffic patterns; inspect which model and how many tokens per request.
  5. Root cause: A long-lived secret was placed in a client I do not control, with no per-user limits or server-side checks.
  6. Fix: A small backend proxy: app -> HTTPS + user auth token -> my backend -> LLM. The backend holds the key in a secret manager, validates the user, applies per-user rate limits and quotas, fixes allowed models and max_tokens, logs usage, and streams SSE back to the app. Add Play Integrity / app attestation to reduce abuse (verify).
  7. Prevention: Secret scanning in CI, separate keys for dev/prod, budget alerts, and a review rule: no provider keys in mobile code, ever.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The proxy adds a hop and ops work (small latency cost), but it is the only safe design; I would not trust client-side obfuscation or let the client choose the model or token limits.
# minimal FastAPI-style proxy sketch
@app.post("/chat")
def chat(req: ChatReq, user=Depends(auth)):
    quota.check(user.id)                       # per-user limit
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
                               messages=req.messages[-20:])
    quota.add(user.id, r.usage.input_tokens + r.usage.output_tokens)
    return {"text": r.content[0].text}
// Android side: call YOUR endpoint, never the provider
val req = Request.Builder().url("https://api.example.com/chat")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer $userToken").post(body).build()
// Spring controller sketch for the proxy
@PostMapping("/chat")
public Map<String,String> chat(@RequestBody ChatReq req, Principal user) {
    quota.check(user.getName());
    Message m = client.messages().create(buildParams(req));   // key lives in server env var
    return Map.of("text", firstText(m));
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the proxy is abused with valid accounts? → Per-user quotas, anomaly alerts, account bans.
  • On-device models instead? → Removes the key problem for simple tasks but with quality/size trade-offs (later topic).
  • Is a short-lived token minted by the backend OK for direct calls? → Only if the provider supports scoped ephemeral tokens (verify); otherwise proxy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A key in an APK was found by a scraper within days; the team's first reaction was obfuscation, which delayed the real fix by a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: obfuscation.
  • Hire: rotate key and add a proxy.
  • Strong hire: quotas, attestation, streaming proxy, kill switch for old builds and secret scanning.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test code that calls an LLM, given it is slow, paid and non-deterministic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production teams need CI that is fast and free, plus a separate quality signal for the model itself.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I split testing into two layers. Unit tests use a fake client with canned responses to check my own logic: history trimming, retries, error handling, parsing, cost maths. Evaluation runs call the real model on a small labelled set and measure pass rates against thresholds, separately and less often. I never assert exact text from the live model in CI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layer 1 (deterministic, free, fast): inject an Llm interface (see the pinning question) and use a fake that can also simulate failures: 429 then success, truncation (max_tokens), a mid-stream error, malformed JSON. Verify that retries happen exactly where intended, that a failed call removes the dangling user message, and that the system prompt survives trimming.

Layer 2 (statistical): 50 to 200 representative inputs with expected outputs or rubrics; score by exact label, regex, schema validity or an LLM-as-judge (later topic); run on prompt/model changes and nightly; fail the build if the pass rate drops below the baseline. Record cost and latency alongside.

Also keep a few recorded real responses as fixtures for parser tests, and contract tests that run rarely against the real API to detect SDK/API drift.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FakeClient:
    def __init__(self, replies): self.replies, self.calls = list(replies), 0
    def create(self, **kw):
        self.calls += 1
        r = self.replies.pop(0)
        if isinstance(r, Exception): raise r
        return r

def test_removes_dangling_user_turn_on_error():
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]
    try: call_model(FakeClient([RuntimeError("boom")]), history)
    except RuntimeError: history.pop()
    assert history == []
class FakeLlm(private val replies: ArrayDeque<Result<String>>) : Llm {
    var calls = 0
    override fun complete(system: String, messages: List<Pair<String, String>>, maxTokens: Int): Pair<String, Usage> {
        calls++
        return replies.removeFirst().getOrThrow() to Usage(1, 1)
    }
}
// test: FakeLlm(ArrayDeque(listOf(Result.failure(RuntimeException()), Result.success("ok")))) then assert retry logic
class FakeLlm implements Llm {
    private final Deque<Object> replies; int calls = 0;
    FakeLlm(Object... r) { replies = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(r)); }
    public Result complete(String system, List<Msg> messages, int maxTokens) {
        calls++;
        Object r = replies.removeFirst();
        if (r instanceof RuntimeException e) throw e;
        return new Result((String) r, 1, 1);
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CI that calls the real paid API on every commit.
  • Exact-string assertions on model output.
  • No failure simulation, so error paths ship untested.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How large should the eval set be? → Start with 50 representative cases; grow with each production bug.
  2. How handle flaky evals? → Run multiple samples and use thresholds, fix temperature, report confidence.
  3. What goes in nightly vs per-PR? → Per-PR: fakes plus a small smoke eval; nightly: the full eval and cost report.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: mocks the API or manually tries prompts. Senior: two-layer testing, failure injection, thresholds on eval pass rates, cost/latency tracking and regression cases added from incidents.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A prompt tweak that "looked fine" dropped a classifier from 94 to 81 percent on the eval set; the CI gate blocked it before release.
